items.prompt: Which one uses electricity?

options.why: A kite is moved by the wind.
A book does not need electricity.
A broom is moved by a person.

hints: Think about things that plug into the wall.
Which one would stop working in a power cut?
Ask: which one keeps food cold?
items.explanation: A fridge uses electricity to keep food cold. A kite, a book and a broom do not need electricity.

items.prompt: Does it use electricity? Sort the cards.
hints: Things that use electricity need a plug or batteries.
Ask: would it still work in a power cut with no batteries?
Start with the rice cooker. Does it have a plug?
items.explanation: A TV, a rice cooker, a fan and a torch use electricity. A bicycle, a drum and a pencil do not.

items.prompt: Mains or batteries? Sort the cards.
hints: Big machines usually plug into the wall.
Small things we carry often use batteries.
Start with the TV remote. Does it have a cable?
items.explanation: A fridge, a washing machine and an electric kettle plug into the wall for mains electricity. A TV remote, a torch and a wall clock use batteries.

items.prompt: Which one is safe to do?

options.text: Touch a switch with wet hands.
options.why: Water and electricity are a dangerous mix. Dry your hands first.

options.text: Push a pencil into a socket.
options.why: Never put anything into a socket.

options.text: Ask an adult to plug things in.
Pull a plug out by its cable.
options.why: Pulling the cable can break it. An adult should hold the plug itself.

hints: Three of these could give someone a shock.
Think about water, sockets and cables.
Ask: which choice keeps you away from danger?
items.explanation: Asking an adult to plug things in is safe. Wet hands, poking things into sockets and pulling cables can all be dangerous.

items.prompt: Choose all the safe rules for electricity.

options.text: Keep drinks away from a computer.
Fly kites far from power lines.
Dry your hands before touching a switch.
Climb an electricity pole to get a kite.
options.why: Never climb an electricity pole. Ask an adult for help.

options.text: Use a hairdryer in the bath.
options.why: Never use electrical things near water. It can give a dangerous shock.

hints: Water and electricity must be kept apart.
Power lines carry very strong electricity.
Start with the drinks. What could happen if a drink spills on a computer?
items.explanation: Keeping drinks away from computers, flying kites far from power lines and drying your hands are safe rules. Never climb poles or use electrical things near water.

items.prompt: A torch gets its electricity from a ___.

figure.alt: A torch with its back opened.

hints: You can buy them in sizes like AA.
A TV remote uses the same thing.
items.explanation: A torch gets electricity from batteries. Batteries store a small amount of electricity.

items.prompt: Why is mains electricity more dangerous than a small battery?

options.why: Mains electricity is not hot. It is much stronger than a battery.
Electricity is not wet. Water can carry it to you.
Noise is not the danger. Its strength is.

hints: Think about what mains electricity can power.
A battery runs a torch. The mains runs a washing machine.
Ask: which one has more power behind it?
items.explanation: Mains electricity is much stronger than a small battery. It can give a very dangerous shock, so we never play with sockets.

items.prompt: Which bulb will light up?

figure.alt: A battery and a bulb with a gap in the wire.

options.why: There is a gap, so electricity cannot flow all the way round.

figure.alt: A battery and a bulb joined in a complete loop of wire.
A battery, a bulb and an open switch.

options.why: The switch is open, so there is a gap in the circuit.

figure.alt: A bulb and a closed switch with no battery.

options.why: There is no battery, so there is no electricity.

hints: A bulb needs a battery and a complete loop.
Look for gaps and open switches.
Check each circuit: is there a battery? Is there a gap?
items.explanation: The bulb lights when there is a battery and the wires make a complete loop with no gaps.

items.prompt: What does a switch do in a circuit?

figure.alt: A circuit with a battery, a lit bulb and a closed switch.

options.why: A switch does not change the battery.

options.text: It changes the colour of the bulb.
options.why: A switch turns the bulb on or off. It does not change colour.

options.text: It opens or closes a gap in the circuit.

options.why: Batteries store electricity. A switch opens or closes the circuit.

hints: Think about the light switch in your room.
What happens to the bulb when you press the switch?
Ask: what does a gap in a circuit do?
items.explanation: A switch opens or closes a gap in the circuit. When it is closed, electricity flows and the bulb lights. When it is open, the bulb goes off.

items.prompt: Match each object to where it gets its electricity.
hints: Some things use batteries and some use the mains.
A phone has a battery that needs charging.
Start with the fridge. Where is its plug?
items.explanation: A TV remote uses small batteries and a fridge plugs into the mains. A phone's battery is charged from a socket, and a solar lamp uses sunlight.

items.prompt: A power line has fallen down after a storm. What should Bayu do?

figure.alt: A power line lying on the ground after a storm.

options.why: Never go near a fallen power line, even with a stick.
Stay far away. The wire may still carry electricity.

options.text: Pick it up and move it.
options.why: Never touch a fallen power line.

options.text: Stay far away and tell an adult.

hints: Power lines carry very strong electricity.
A fallen wire may still be live.
Ask: which choice keeps Bayu far away from the wire?
items.explanation: A fallen power line can still carry electricity. Bayu should stay far away and tell an adult, who can call for help.

items.prompt: Why must we keep water away from plugs and sockets?

options.why: Water does not switch electricity off. It can carry it.

options.text: Water can carry electricity into your body.

options.why: Cold is not the danger. Water can carry electricity.

options.text: Water is too heavy for plugs.
options.why: Weight is not the danger. Water can carry electricity.

hints: Think about why bathrooms have special rules for electricity.
Ask: what could happen if wet hands touch a socket?
items.explanation: Water can carry electricity. If water touches a plug or a socket, electricity could flow through the water into your body and give a shock.

head: Object
Power

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to make the bulb light up.
items: Join a wire to one end of the battery.
Join that wire to the bulb.
Join a second wire from the bulb to the other end of the battery.
hints: The electricity starts at the battery.
The wires must make a complete loop.
Start at the battery. What do you join to it first?
items.explanation: Join a wire from the battery to the bulb, then a second wire from the bulb back to the battery. The loop is complete, so the bulb lights up.

items.prompt: The bulb is not lit. Which change will make it light?

figure.alt: A circuit with a battery, an unlit bulb and an open switch.

options.why: Without a battery, there is no electricity.
A gap stops the electricity flowing.
An open switch makes a gap. Closing it completes the circuit.

hints: Look at the switch in the picture.
An open switch leaves a gap in the circuit.
Ask: how can the gap be closed?
items.explanation: The switch is open, so there is a gap. Closing the switch completes the circuit, and the bulb lights up.

criteria.label: Draws a clear picture of one safety rule
Writes the rule in a short sentence
The rule is correct and safe

hints: Think about water, sockets or power lines.

items.explanation: Electricity can hurt us. Good rules are: never touch switches with wet hands, never poke things into sockets and fly kites far from power lines.

It opens and closes a gap in the circuit.
Most lights at home have one on the wall.
items.explanation: A switch opens or closes the circuit. When it is closed, electricity can flow.

A bicycle uses your legs.

hints: Which one has parts that move by themselves?

A circuit does not need a book.

items.prompt: Which material lets electricity pass through easily?

options.why: Plastic stops electricity.
Wood stops electricity.
Rubber stops electricity.

hints: Plastic is used to cover wires.
items.explanation: Metals such as copper let electricity pass through. This is why wires are metal.

items.prompt: Why is a cable covered with plastic?

options.why: Safety is the reason.
It is not for weight.
Cables are not eaten.

hints: Touching a bare wire is dangerous.
items.explanation: Plastic does not let electricity pass through. It keeps us safe when we touch the cable.

items.prompt: Which child is being safe with a plug?

options.text: Cara pulls the plug out by the wire.
options.why: This can damage the wire.

options.why: Water is dangerous with electricity.

options.text: Ben holds the plug to pull it out.
Eli pokes a fork into a socket.
options.why: This is very dangerous.

items.explanation: Pull a plug out by holding the plug, not the wire. Keep water away from electricity.
